summary: Shows how the BGP community attribute can make routing policy easier to set up for customers connected to several providers. It is an informational example of how to use communities, not a new protocol.

how to use bgp communities for routing policy
subtitle: Using BGP community attributes to manage routing policy in multihomed networks.

tldr.problem: In multihomed networks where customers connect to multiple providers, providers need to customize BGP routing policies for each customer. Configuring this on a per-AS basis creates scalability and management problems.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of having providers customize LOCAL_PREF values for each customer AS, customers can tag their route announcements with community values. Providers apply uniform community-to-LOCAL_PREF mappings, letting customers control their own routing policy without requiring provider customization.
tldr.outcome: Community-based configuration is easier to manage and scale, lets customers control their routing directly, and enables per-prefix granularity instead of just per-AS. MCI demonstrated successful deployment with positive customer response.

today: RFC 1998 is an Informational document describing a practical technique for managing BGP routing policy in multihomed networks. It documents real-world deployment by MCI and has proven influential in showing how existing BGP tools can simplify network operations. The community-based approach has become a standard practice for ISPs and multihomed customers managing complex routing policies.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Statement
sections.content:
In the multihomed Internet, it is common for customers to have connections to multiple service providers or redundant paths for reliability. Achieving desired routing policies requires coordination between customers and providers, typically resulting in customized BGP LOCAL_PREF configuration at the provider routers.

When many customers require customization, this becomes a scalability and management burden for providers. Customization is often done on a per-AS basis for efficiency, but this prevents prefix-level policy granularity. RFC 1998 shows how the BGP community attribute can simplify this by shifting the responsibility for policy configuration from the provider to the customer.
sections.plainLanguage: Large ISPs struggle when each customer wants their traffic routed differently. Communities let customers handle their own preferences without the ISP having to change everything.

sections.title: The BGP Community Attribute
sections.content:
The BGP community path attribute is an optional transitive attribute consisting of four-octet values, each specifying a community. Community values are encoded using an AS number in the first two octets with the remaining two octets defined by that AS. A community is a group of destination prefixes that share some common attribute. Each prefix can belong to multiple communities.

Well-known communities like NO_EXPORT (0xFFFFFF01) and NO_ADVERTISE (0xFFFFFF02) have predefined meanings. The community attribute allows routers to group prefixes and make routing decisions based on community membership, providing a flexible mechanism for expressing routing policy.
sections.plainLanguage: A community is a tag you attach to routes: it is a number that encodes an AS number plus a policy code. Routers can then look for routes with specific tags and handle them accordingly.

sections.title: Community-Based Configuration Approach
sections.content:
With community-based configuration, a provider first coordinates with its customers to establish a mapping between community values and BGP LOCAL_PREF values. The provider applies a uniform BGP configuration to all customers that matches routes by community values and sets LOCAL_PREF accordingly.

Customers requiring customized LOCAL_PREF configuration simply tag their route announcements with the appropriate community values. This can be done based on AS paths or IP address access lists. The major advantages include customer control over their own routing policy, ability to achieve per-prefix customization (without AS-path manipulation), addressing provider scalability by distributing configuration work to customers who need customization, and simpler provider configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider says: if you tag routes with community 3561:70, I'll set LOCAL_PREF to 70. Customers tag their routes, and the provider's uniform configuration does the rest.

sections.title: Real-World Implementation at MCI
sections.content:
MCI implemented this technique with several community-to-LOCAL_PREF mappings: community 3561:70 (0x0DE90046) maps to LOCAL_PREF 70 (primary via another ISP), 3561:80 (0x0DE90050) maps to LOCAL_PREF 80 (dual-homed), and 3561:90 (0x0DE9005A) maps to LOCAL_PREF 90 (customer backup routes). The default LOCAL_PREF of 100 is applied to untagged customer routes.

Customers can configure community tagging based on either AS path lists or IP address access lists, enabling them to apply different policies to different portions of their network. MCI applies a uniform route-map to all customers, creating a highly scalable approach. The technique was tested in production with positive customer response and MCI has been migrating existing AS-based customizations to this community-based approach.
sections.plainLanguage: MCI says: use community 3561:90 for backup routes, 3561:80 for dual-homed routes, 3561:70 for using another ISP first. Each customer picks which communities to use on their own routes.
